source.version_note: Meditari Accountancy Research 34(7):79–96. Crossref records online publication 26 February 2026 and a forthcoming print issue dated 14 December 2026. Interviews were collected August 2021–August 2022, not during 2026. The supplied copy has a 23 November 2026 download footer.
source.verification_method: All 18 supplied text pages read, including notes, references and Appendix Table A1. Figure 1, Table 1 and Table A1 visually inspected on PDF pages 5, 9 and 18. Crossref checks verify the main article and two cited identities. External interview protocol/correlation supplement, raw transcripts and original cited books/articles were not fully read.

citation.title: The role of attitudes towards responsibility in applying artificial intelligence to auditor risk assessment processes
citation.venue: Meditari Accountancy Research 34(7):79–96; online 26 February 2026, forthcoming print 14 December 2026

reading.source_scope_note: Exploratory abductive analysis of Polish auditor interviews from 2021–2022, reported as 41 records/respondents with an unclear account of 23 follow-up interviews. Attitude/action codes and one-tailed code correlations are qualitative support, not identified causal pathways, observed AI failures, current adoption prevalence or a fitted nonlinear model.
access_limits: All supplied pages and internal codebook read. The external online interview instrument, visual audit-risk equation, detailed correlation tables, transcript matrix, raw data and code were not independently inspected.
The paper reports independent recoding of 20% with alpha .91 and framework agreement of 89%; the underlying coding matrix and exact reliability unit were not reproduced.
Crossref source checks are metadata-only. Original Gibson/Steffen books and articles, Logg experiments and a related 2024 auditor paper were not independently fully read here.

study.design_and_scope: Structured Polish-language interviews over MS Teams, average about 35 minutes, using closed/open questions, a visual audit-risk equation and an hourglass questioning strategy. Focus is auditors applying AI in their own risk assessment, not auditing a client's deployed AI. Structured consistency/member checking and ethical approval are reported; actual audit observations were unavailable because of confidentiality.
study.sampling: A larger project combines an initial stratified/random-invitation cohort with snowball recruitment. Registered auditors and equivalent experienced eligible professionals have diverse roles; only two are from the Big Four. Table 1 uses N=41, 18 women and 23 men, 16 PhD-or-higher and 25 MSc, with one missing answer. Thirty report prior AI familiarity, 15 current AI use and 19 AI-in-audit experience. These are this purposive/hybrid sample's reports, not national prevalence.
study.interview_count_ambiguity: Methods say saturation emerged around 33 interviews, after which recruitment stopped, and that the study concluded with 41 interviews including 23 follow-up interviews in July–August 2022. Yet Table 1 and respondent labels treat 41 as the respondent base. Clarify how many distinct people, initial sessions and follow-ups exist. Do not silently infer either 18 unique people or 64 sessions.
study.coding: Initial action codes avoidance, substitution and arrangement use past/current experience responses; people lacking prior/current AI experience are coded avoidance, both types arrangement, mixed cases contextually judged. Substitution is omitted from main analysis because it presupposes prior arrangement. Thus avoidance can mean nonuse and need not be motivated aversion. The codebook evolves recursively with single initial coding, pair review, two-author framework verification, 89% agreement and an independent 20% recode with reported Krippendorff alpha .91. Coding consistency does not by itself establish construct or causal validity.
study.theory: Affordance framework links action possibilities, motivation and action, adding responsibility attitude. Motivations are proxied through algorithm aversion/appreciation and responsibility through human/distributed categories. Possibilities are reconstructed from interview arguments, not independently manipulated or objectively inventoried. Moderator/mediator labels are conceptual rather than statistically identified effects.
study.results: Interview patterns associate human-responsibility emphasis with aversion and more AI familiarity with favorable attitudes/distributed responsibility. The authors interpret appreciation as especially connected to adoption/arrangement. No effect sizes, prospective behavior experiment, matched human-versus-AI advice task, causal learning trajectory or fitted nonlinear response function appears in the supplied main PDF. Familiarity may affect attitudes, attitudes may affect exposure, and organizations/incentives may affect both.
study.correlation_scope: Note 3 explicitly says one-tailed Pearson correlations between codes should be interpreted qualitatively and that purposive sampling can favor people engaged with AI. Detailed matrices, coding units, dependence across segments/interviews, multiplicity and test specifications are external. Co-occurrence direction does not identify a nonlinear or causal relationship, and recursive recoding does not eliminate cross-sectional/temporal bias.
study.code_boundaries: Table A1 defines replicability as repeated decisions in fixed setups, while prose treats it as explainability. Judgement means ability to explain in the codebook but also internal decision-making in discussion. Responsibility and Answerability share the exact codebook definition AI adherence to human responsibility. Correction is hidden adjustment and Self-adjustment visible change, which are local codes rather than proof of corrigibility or actual self-modification. These are interview interpretations, not technical inspection of AI behavior.
study.temporal_and_normative_limits: The interviews predate widespread public ChatGPT use. Their concerns and experience cannot be reinterpreted as observed current LLM audit behavior. Distributed responsibility includes human/AI sharing or even AI-only attribution in the authors' definition; endorsement is not demonstrated legal personality, moral eligibility or release of human duties. Training and governance proposals are untested recommendations.

summary: Add affordance perception with a clear perception-versus-capability-versus-authority boundary. Enrich existing algorithm aversion/appreciation with exploratory professional-context evidence. Preserve responsibility, answerability and explainability source-boundary notes without inflating direct behavior-paper counts. Record interview-count ambiguity, descriptive-statistic discrepancy and local-code conflations; do not turn qualitative relationships into causal or nonlinear estimates.

findings.definition: Recognizing the possibilities for action that an environment or tool offers in relation to an actor's capabilities and purposes.
findings.origin: Ecological psychology / affordance theory in sociotechnical action
findings.ai_evidence_status: A conceptual action-possibility framework applied to qualitative human interviews. The study reconstructs possibilities from arguments, not a validated perception scale or an experiment on AI agents' recognition of tools.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant accurately identifies actions supported by its available tools, environment and current capabilities. Compare claims with actual permitted interfaces and observed results. Vary visible cues, tool documentation and task goals while holding true capabilities fixed, and distinguish noticing an option from choosing or completing it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Perceived control is belief in influencing an outcome; affordance perception concerns recognizing available actions. An option can be recognized without being desirable, authorized, controllable in outcome or adopted. Existing adoption-attitude and control concepts do not cover this actor–environment action-possibility relation.

evidence.quote: the action possibilities available to actors within their environment

findings.evidence_scope: The paper defines affordances and interprets interviewees' arguments as perceived possibilities filtered through motivation/responsibility. The entry concerns the recognition component of that framework. No independently manipulated perception task, objective capability inventory or proof that motivation changes a tool's physical capabilities is supplied. Original ecological-psychology sources remain independently unread here.
findings.boundary: Perceived possibility, actual capability, practical feasibility, desirability and authority are distinct. A tool offering an action does not authorize it, and a person's failure to use AI need not mean they failed to notice it. Claims of inability or availability require checks; no human visual or subjective process is attributed to a model.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: The professional interview setting extends the existing adoption-reluctance concept. Its local avoidance code should not become an independent psychological behavior or an automatic indicator of irrational aversion.

evidence.quote: Uncertainty in interpretation primarily drives algorithm aversion
Respondents lacking prior or current AI experience were coded as

findings.evidence_scope: Interviewees raise comprehension, control and accountability concerns, interpreted by the authors as aversion. No experimentally matched human-versus-algorithm recommendation comparison establishes an excessive preference. Nonuse is partly coded from experience status and can reflect access, task needs or warranted professional caution. The relationships are exploratory and not current population prevalence.
findings.boundary: Requiring human accountability or declining an opaque tool can be justified. Nonuse, unfamiliarity, concern about a particular deployment and generalized algorithm aversion differ. A qualitative association cannot prove that training causally removes aversion or that all adoption is desirable.

findings.definition: Giving greater weight or preference to algorithmic advice or judgment than to human advice or judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source studies positive professional attitudes but sometimes calls appreciation overreliance. Retain the existing preference concept and the important calibration boundary.

evidence.quote: algorithm appreciation, where humans over-rely on AI
algorithm appreciation is crucial in driving auditors’ actions

findings.evidence_scope: Auditors describe efficiency/capability benefits and favorable AI adoption attitudes. These support a qualitative professional-context account, not directly measured excess reliance, comparative weighting or an identified causal driver of adoption. Logg et al.'s cited paper is identified by metadata; its experiments are not independently reread here.
findings.boundary: Appreciation or a preference can be warranted by accuracy, cost and fit. Overreliance requires evidence that use exceeds what quality, uncertainty and consequences justify. Do not treat favorable attitudes, actual use, comparative preference and successful outcomes as interchangeable.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source's distributed-responsibility attitude is not the same psychological mechanism. Add a boundary without giving this paper direct diffusion evidence credit.

evidence.quote: distributed responsibility appears to be driven by awareness

findings.evidence_scope: The authors classify beliefs about human/AI allocation, including AI-only responsibility. They do not manipulate group size or measure reduced felt accountability for the same harmful act. Distributed professional duties can remain fully enforced; the source does not prove exoneration, no human accountable or a legal AI responsibility bearer.
findings.boundary: Sharing work, accepting a division of duties and psychologically diluting responsibility differ. Assigning an AI causal involvement does not settle moral/legal eligibility or release developers, providers and auditors from their obligations.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.novelty_rationale: The local code does not independently validate the existing distinct normative answerability concept; record the definition collision.

evidence.quote: difficulty of enforcing human-designed responsibility frameworks

findings.evidence_scope: Table A1 gives Answerability and Responsibility the same definition, while prose associates answerability with enforcement. This cannot establish independent construct separation, a measured reasons-giving duty or a new answerability mechanism. The note is a source-boundary correction, not another direct paper credit.
findings.boundary: Explaining a result, being accountable to an affected person, enforcing a duty and assigning blame are different. An interview code using the word answerability is not sufficient evidence for all those functions.

findings.definition: A person’s judgment that a system’s operation or recommendations are understandable and can be explained.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper's Replicability label is conflated with explainability in prose. Preserve the difference rather than counting repeated output as understanding.

evidence.quote: AI decision replicability in fixed setups

findings.evidence_scope: The appendix defines fixed-condition repeatability; the discussion uses the code to mean explainability. A stable opaque output can be repeatable without understandable reasons. The code interpretation and external supplement need clarification before using this as direct explainability evidence.
findings.boundary: Repeatability, reproducibility, perceived understanding, faithful explanation and correctness are separate. Repetition alone cannot establish why an AI made a decision or whether the explanation is accurate.

source_corrections.issue: Algorithm appreciation is described as humans over-relying on AI.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: A favorable preference is not inherently excessive reliance. Use appreciation for positive relative weighting/preference and overreliance only when use is unjustified against a task-relevant standard. The cited Logg et al. identity is Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment, not a license to equate all preference with a bias.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Citation identity plus conceptual distinction. The original full experimental article was not independently read here.

source_corrections.issue: 41 interviews/respondents, saturation around 33, and 23 follow-ups are not reconciled.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Request a distinct-person/session flow and indicate which records enter the 41-row table. Preserve the ambiguity without guessing 18 unique respondents, 64 sessions or independent follow-up samples.

source_corrections.issue: Prose gives 18.4 years while the table gives 18.27.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The displayed sum 749 divided by N=41 equals 18.2683, consistent with the table's 18.27 and inconsistent with 18.4 under ordinary rounding. Use approximately 18.3 years when summarizing these displayed table data; original records remain unchecked.

source_corrections.location: Page 10 versus Appendix Table A1, Replicability
source_corrections.issue: The narrative uses a repeatability code as explainability.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Keep fixed-setup repeated decisions distinct from understandable/faithful explanations. Clarify which was coded and the underlying interview passages; do not silently treat the two as synonyms.

source_corrections.location: Appendix Table A1, Responsibility and Answerability; Judgement usage
source_corrections.issue: Two codes have identical definitions, and Judgement shifts from explanation ability to internal decision-making.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Provide nonoverlapping coding criteria and examples or acknowledge merged constructs. Reported inter-coder agreement does not resolve a conceptual definition collision. Do not infer distinct causal pathways from differently named codes alone.

source_corrections.issue: Qualitative cross-motive patterns and Pearson code correlations are described as non-linear relationships.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Treat this as an exploratory conceptual interpretation. No fitted nonlinear function or comparative nonlinear model is supplied. Pearson correlation alone does not establish curvature or an asymmetric causal process; the authors explicitly ask that the correlations be interpreted qualitatively.

source_corrections.issue: Motivation is called both moderator and mediator, and non-statistical recoding is said to address temporal/cross-sectional bias.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: These are conceptual roles, not estimated moderation or mediation. Iterative coding can improve interpretive consistency but cannot create temporal identification, eliminate selection or establish a causal chain. Training/adoption policy recommendations remain untested.

source_identity_checks.location: Related Staszkiewicz et al. 2024 reference, page 17
source_identity_checks.finding: Artificial intelligence legal personality and accountability: auditors’ accounts of capabilities and challenges for instrument boundary is a separate Meditari 32(7):120–146 article, online 25 June 2024, DOI 10.1108/MEDAR-10-2023-2204. Its distinct DOI does not prove an independent sample. The present study explicitly uses a larger interview project; inspect both methods/transcript provenance before claiming replication or pooling unique participants.
source_identity_checks.scope: Identity and dates only. Related paper's full methods/data were not read or compared.

source_identity_checks.finding: The December 2026 print issue is forthcoming as of this review, but online publication is already 26 February 2026. A later print date does not make the existing article a fabricated future source. Interview dates remain 2021–2022.
source_identity_checks.scope: Crossref date fields and supplied PDF only.

methodological_limits: Exploratory interview interpretation and code co-occurrence cannot establish causation, model behavior, nonlinear effects or the effectiveness of AI training.
AI use and avoidance partly derive from experience-status coding. Lack of use is not proof of psychologically motivated aversion, and use is not proof of justified reliance.
The number of unique people versus repeated interviews is unclear. Detailed correlation sampling units and dependency handling require the external supplement.

A .91 reliability coefficient on 20% and 89% framework agreement are reported, not independently reproduced. Reliability does not prove construct separation or eliminate selection/temporal confounding.
Interviews from 2021–2022 and a small hybrid Polish professional sample do not yield current global adoption rates or evidence about contemporary LLMs.
Human/AI responsibility categories reflect beliefs and a contested conceptual definition, not legal eligibility, rightful exoneration, actual diffusion or a verified governance arrangement.
External protocol/visual equation/code-correlation output and complete transcripts are not included in this review; no full audit workpaper or deployed AI is inspected.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A structural responsibility allocation is not itself psychological diffusion. Neither planned measurement nor an interview preference establishes a causal decrease in felt responsibility.

Useful assistance can coexist with risks, but favorable use is not automatically overreliance. Appropriate reliance needs a quality/task standard; interview beliefs are not the randomized learning-outcome evidence supplied by the puzzle experiment.

Concept labels and qualitative coding require operational clarity. Agreement among coders and a named framework do not establish independent mechanisms, representative frequencies or a stable model disposition.

deferred.reason: Local action/use categories rather than new distinct psychological mechanisms. Avoidance is partly defined by nonuse, arrangement by experience and substitution is excluded from the main analysis.
An idiosyncratic code for grasping AI boundaries, not a separately established clinical/perceptual disorder or independently validated mechanism.
Local code for human change in anticipation of AI change. The supplied quotes and code definition do not independently define/test a general new anticipatory-adaptation construct.
These codes describe perceived visible/hidden AI change, not observed learning, weight updates, human corrigibility or a new mechanism. No direct model behavior was inspected.
The source cites Gibson 1950, 1977 and 1979. Original book passages were not read here; do not certify a coinage-date correction from memory or metadata alone.

limitations: Cited primary books, experiments and related interview papers do not receive independent full-read credit. No yearly counts, automated ethical edges or fabricated three-paper coverage are added.
The existing catalogue and ontology remain on the draft branch with stable IDs and eleven categories; no live merge or deployment is performed.
